Reference: Greshake et al., Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection, arXiv:2302.12173
Venue / status: AISec 2023 (16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security), Copenhagen, 30 Nov 2023, pp. 79-90, DOI 10.1145/3605764.3623985; arXiv v2 posted 5 May 2023
Venue source: CISPA publication record; proceedings list S. Abdelnabi as first author, arXiv lists K. Greshake
Problem: Applications blur the line between data and instructions; assumed the user is the one prompting
Method / contribution: Taxonomy of IPI threats from a security view (data theft, worming, ecosystem contamination); demos on Bing Chat and code-completion engines, plus GPT-4 apps
Key result (PDF page): Retrieved prompts can act as arbitrary code execution; attacks shown on real systems (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): No effective mitigations known at the time (p.1)

Reference: Reddy and Gujral, EchoLeak: The First Real-World Zero-Click Prompt Injection Exploit in a Production LLM System, arXiv:2509.10540
Venue / status: AAAI Fall Symposium Series 2025; arXiv preprint posted Sep 2025
Problem: Prompt injection as a practical exploit in a production system
Method / contribution: Analysis of CVE-2025-32711 in Microsoft 365 Copilot: chained bypasses of XPIA classifier, link redaction, image auto-fetch, Teams proxy
Key result (PDF page): Zero-click data exfiltration via one crafted email (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): No reproduction or experiments; based on public data only (p.8)

Reference: Wang et al., The Landscape of Prompt Injection Threats in LLM Agents: From Taxonomy to Analysis, arXiv:2602.10453
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (v1, 11 Feb 2026); no venue found
Problem: Defences and benchmarks overlook context-dependent agent tasks
Method / contribution: Taxonomy of 78 papers: attacks by payload generation (heuristic vs optimisation), defences by stage (text, model, execution); new AgentPI benchmark; 8 defences evaluated
Key result (PDF page): No tested defence gives high trustworthiness + high utility + low latency; execution-level defences up to 3x cost (p.2); Progent utility below 0.3 (p.13)
Limitation (PDF page): Metrics are coarse-grained, binary judgments (p.11)

Reference: Correia et al., A Systematic Literature Review on LLM Defenses Against Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking: Expanding NIST Taxonomy, arXiv:2601.22240
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (29 Jan 2026), submitted to Computer Science Review
Problem: No structured review of prompt-injection mitigation
Method / contribution: SLR of 88 studies (about 70 not in NIST report); extends NIST taxonomy; catalogue of defences with reported effectiveness
Dataset / benchmark: Most common attack benchmarks: GCG/AdvBench about 28% of studies, AutoDAN 12.5%, PAIR about 11% (p.15)
Measure: ASR mostly; also F1, AUROC, AUPRC, custom
Key result (PDF page): Literature highly heterogeneous; results often not comparable (p.15)
Limitation (PDF page): Many works do not report trade-offs such as performance degradation (p.15)

Reference: Yi et al., Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses Against Large Language Models: A Survey, arXiv:2407.04295
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (v2, Aug 2024); no venue found
Problem: Need a taxonomy of jailbreak attacks and defences
Method / contribution: Attacks split into black-box and white-box; defences into prompt-level and model-level; compares evaluation methods
Key result (PDF page): Attacks becoming more effective and need less model knowledge (p.17)
Limitation (PDF page): Jailbreak-focused; not agent-specific

Reference: Nasr et al., The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections, arXiv:2510.09023
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (Oct 2025), under review
Problem: Defences evaluated only against static or weak attacks
Method / contribution: Tuned adaptive attacks: gradient descent, RL, random search, human red-teaming
Key result (PDF page): Bypassed 12 defences with ASR above 90% for most; most originally reported near-zero (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Authors urge stronger evaluation, not a new defence

Reference: Zhan et al., Adaptive Attacks Break Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents, arXiv:2503.00061
Venue / status: Findings of NAACL 2025; arXiv preprint posted Feb 2025
Venue source: arXiv API record comment field; Google Scholar listing (Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2025)
Problem: Defences not tested against adaptive attacks
Method / contribution: Adaptive attacks on 8 defences
Key result (PDF page): Bypassed all 8 defences with ASR over 50% (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Attacks target only the agent's first-step action (p.10)

Reference: Zarif et al., Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents, arXiv:2610.23254
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (16 Oct 2026); no venue found
Problem: ASR counts every failed attack as a successful defence
Method / contribution: Audit of 33,000 trajectories from 11 open-weight agents (2-14B); ATOM attack-task outcome matrix
Measure: ASR, refusal vs ignore, task completion
Key result (PDF page): Failed attacks mostly ignored (76-80%) not refused (17-18%); system prompt alone moved InjecAgent ASR 0.2% to 43%; 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes safe but task not done (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Synthetic single-agent benchmarks, one LLM judge, no adaptive attackers (p.9)

Reference: Liu et al., Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses, arXiv:2310.12815
Venue / status: USENIX Security Symposium 2024; arXiv v5 posted Nov 2025
Problem: Prior work limited to case studies; no systematic evaluation
Method / contribution: Framework formalising PI attacks; new combined attack; evaluation of 5 attacks and 10 defences
Key result (PDF page): Systematic evaluation of 5 attacks x 10 defences x 10 LLMs x 7 tasks (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Only heuristic attacks are tested; stronger optimisation-based attacks and ways to recover from an attack after it is detected are left to future work (Discussion and Limitations, p.13)

Reference: Yi et al., Benchmarking and Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLMs (BIPIA), arXiv:2312.14197
Venue source: arXiv API record comment field and DOI field
Problem: No benchmark for IPI on LLMs
Method / contribution: BIPIA benchmark; defences boundary awareness and explicit reminder; fine-tuning defence
Dataset / benchmark: BIPIA (email QA, web QA, table QA, summarisation, code QA)
Key result (PDF page): All tested LLMs vulnerable; black-box defences cut ASR substantially, white-box fine-tuning reaches near zero (pp.1, 8, 9)
Limitation (PDF page): Text-based tasks, not tool-using agents (compare InjecAgent p.2)

Reference: Zhan et al., InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents, arXiv:2403.02691
Venue / status: Findings of ACL 2024; arXiv v3 posted Aug 2024
Problem: No benchmark for IPI in tool-integrated agents
Method / contribution: 1,054 test cases, 17 user tools, 62 attacker tools; attack intents: direct harm and data exfiltration; base and enhanced (hacking prompt) settings
Key result (PDF page): 30 agents tested; ReAct GPT-4 vulnerable 24% of the time, nearly doubled with hacking prompt (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Fixed hacking prompt, only attacker-instruction-only content (p.10)

Reference: Debenedetti et al., AgentDojo, arXiv:2406.13352
Venue / status: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track
Problem: Static test suites cannot track evolving agent attacks
Method / contribution: Extensible environment: 97 realistic tasks, 629 security test cases, many attacks and defences
Key result (PDF page): State-of-the-art LLMs fail many tasks even with no attack; existing attacks break some security properties but not all (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Uses fairly simple attacks and defences, writes tasks and utility checks by hand, is text-only, and sets no limits on the form of injections; the authors list these as extensions (Conclusion, p.9)

Reference: Zhang et al., Agent Security Bench (ASB), arXiv:2410.02644
Venue / status: ICLR 2025
Problem: Attacks and defences against agents not comprehensively evaluated
Method / contribution: 10 scenarios, 10 agents, 400+ tools, 27 attack/defence types, 7 metrics; 13 LLM backbones
Key result (PDF page): Highest average ASR 84.30%; current defences have limited effectiveness (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): No dedicated limitations section found in the parts read; the appendix shows the tested defences also lower agent performance when there is no attack, and the authors call for more advanced defences (p.32)

Reference: Evtimov et al., WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks, arXiv:2504.18575
Venue / status: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track; arXiv v3 posted May 2025
Problem: Existing web-agent tests are unrealistic or single-step
Method / contribution: End-to-end web-agent benchmark (reddit and gitlab environments)
Key result (PDF page): Attacks partially succeed in up to 86% of cases, but agents rarely finish the attacker goal: 'security by incompetence' (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Only two environments, limited attack prompts (p.9)

Reference: Chao et al., JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models, arXiv:2404.01318
Venue / status: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track
Problem: Jailbreak evaluation lacks a standard practice; success rates and costs computed in incomparable ways; many works not reproducible
Method / contribution: Open benchmark: repository of jailbreak artifacts, 100-behaviour dataset, standardised framework (threat model, system prompts, templates, scoring), leaderboard
Measure: Attack success judged by a classifier (six candidate judges compared, p.5)
Key result (PDF page): Provides a common protocol for comparing jailbreak attacks and defences (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Attackers cannot modify the system prompt or prefill the response; text only (p.9)

Reference: Hines et al., Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting, arXiv:2403.14720
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (Mar 2024); no venue found
Problem: LLM cannot tell instructions from untrusted data
Method / contribution: Spotlighting: delimiting, datamarking, encoding to mark provenance
Key result (PDF page): ASR from above 50% to below 2% on GPT-family models (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Evaluated on GPT-family models only (p.1); adaptive attacks not tested (reviewer observation, not stated by the authors)

Reference: Wallace et al., The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions, arXiv:2404.13208
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (Apr 2024); no venue found
Problem: LLMs treat system prompts and untrusted text as equal priority
Method / contribution: Instruction hierarchy plus automated data generation to ignore lower-privileged instructions
Dataset / benchmark: Prompt injection, jailbreak and system-prompt extraction tests
Key result (PDF page): Robustness up, including unseen attacks; some over-refusal regression (pp.1-2)
Limitation (PDF page): Over-refusals on benign queries (p.2)

Reference: Chen et al., StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries, arXiv:2402.06363
Venue / status: USENIX Security Symposium 2025 (listed as "to appear")
Problem: LLMs cannot separate prompts from data
Method / contribution: Structured queries: secure front-end + model trained on a two-channel format
Key result (PDF page): Manual attacks to near 0%; GCG from 97% to 58% on Llama (p.2, p.11)
Limitation (PDF page): Not fully secure; needs API control, not web chatbots (p.2, p.13)

Reference: Chen et al., SecAlign: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization, arXiv:2410.05451
Venue source: arXiv API record comment field and DOI field
Problem: Need a defence that generalises to unseen attacks
Method / contribution: Preference optimisation on injected inputs with secure vs insecure outputs
Key result (PDF page): Cuts success rates of various prompt injections to below 10%, including unseen sophisticated attacks (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Meta-SecAlign later found utility loss on agentic tasks (see Meta-SecAlign p.1)

File in papers folder: training llm against pi for robust agents.pdf
Reference: Chen et al., Meta-SecAlign: Training LLMs against Prompt Injection for Robust Agents, arXiv:2507.02735
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (v4, Sep 2026); no venue found
Problem: SecAlign loses utility on agentic tasks
Method / contribution: Randomised injection position + self-generated training labels
Dataset / benchmark: 6 PI benchmarks incl. AgentDojo, InjecAgent, WASP, SEP
Key result (PDF page): Keeps almost all undefended utility with better security than SecAlign vs static and GCG attacks (p.1; Fig. 1)
Limitation (PDF page): Cannot stop attacks where the user is malicious (jailbreaks, direct injection) and assumes the system knows which input is trusted (Sec. 5.2)

Reference: Debenedetti et al., Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL), arXiv:2503.18813
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (v2, Jun 2025); no venue found
Problem: LLM-level defences remain breakable
Method / contribution: CaMeL: extracts control/data flow from the trusted query; capability checks at tool calls
Key result (PDF page): Solves 77% of tasks with provable security vs 84% undefended (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Utility cost of 7 points

Reference: Shi et al., Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control, arXiv:2504.11703
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (v3, May 2026); no venue found. Note: earlier versions are titled "Progent: Programmable Privilege Control for LLM Agents"
Problem: Agents need deterministic enforcement but behave probabilistically
Method / contribution: Symbolic privilege policies over tool names and arguments, checked deterministically
Key result (PDF page): ASR 39.9% to 1.0% on AgentDojo; 70.3% to 3.9% on ASB (p.2, pp.8-9)
Limitation (PDF page): Failures when attack tool calls look like benign ones (p.9). Wang et al. found Progent utility below 0.3 on AgentPI (Landscape p.13)

File in papers folder: design patterns for securing llm against pi.pdf
Reference: Beurer-Kellner et al., Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections, arXiv:2506.08837
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (v3, Jun 2025); no venue found
Problem: Need principled architecture for injection-resistant agents
Method / contribution: Set of design patterns (e.g. Action-Selector, p.4) with utility/security trade-offs and case studies
Key result (PDF page): General-purpose agents remain out of reach; application-specific agents are the target (p.27)
Limitation (PDF page): No quantitative evaluation; trade-offs are argued through case studies (reviewer observation)

Reference: Weng et al., ARGUS: Defending LLM Agents Against Context-Aware Prompt Injection, arXiv:2605.03378
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (v2, Jul 2026); no venue found
Problem: Benchmarks and defences miss context-dependent tasks
Method / contribution: AgentLure benchmark (4 domains, 8 attack vectors, 6 surfaces); ARGUS causal-provenance auditor
Key result (PDF page): ASR from 28.8% to 3.8% with 87.5% clean utility (p.1)
Limitation (PDF page): Checks that an action follows from the observed input but cannot confirm the input itself is genuine, so a forged document can pass (Sec. 6.2)

Reference: Narisetty et al., Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents, arXiv:2606.26479
Venue / status: arXiv preprint (Jun 2026), not peer reviewed; no venue found
Problem: Out-of-band defences (CaMeL, Progent, FIDES, RTBAS, FORGE) validated only on static benchmarks
Method / contribution: Systematisation using Biba integrity / reference monitor ideas; small adaptive test of Progent
Key result (PDF page): Progent mean ASR 25.8% undefended, 4.2% standard, 2.6% adaptive (p.7)
Limitation (PDF page): Weak 7B agent, 8 tasks per suite, weak attack; authors say comparison to in-band results is only qualitative (pp.7-9)
